questions.question: In an RSA accumulator, what equation should a correct membership witness w for element x satisfy (using p(x) as x's prime representative)?
questions.explanation: Membership verification checks that raising the witness to the element's prime representative reproduces the accumulator value.

questions.question: Why do accumulator schemes usually map elements to prime representatives (hash-to-prime) instead of using raw integers as exponents?
options: To avoid collisions and ensure clean divisibility structure for witnesses/proofs
To make modular exponentiation faster on CPUs
To guarantee that the accumulator value is a generator
To remove the need for a modulus N entirely
questions.explanation: Prime representatives reduce ambiguity: each element contributes an independent prime factor to the exponent, preventing easy collisions or malleability.

questions.question: If you add a new element z with prime representative p(z), how do you update an existing membership witness w_x for an old element x (append-only set)?
questions.explanation: Witnesses represent the exponent product of all elements except x. Adding z multiplies that product by p(z), which corresponds to exponentiating the witness by p(z).

questions.question: Which statement best captures the main setup difference between RSA accumulators and class group accumulators?
options: RSA accumulators typically require a modulus N whose factorization is unknown (trusted setup), while class group accumulators aim to avoid a hidden-factorization setup
RSA accumulators have constant-size proofs but class group accumulators do not
Class group accumulators only work for non-membership and RSA only for membership
Class group accumulators require pairings but RSA accumulators do not
questions.explanation: Both are unknown-order-group based, but RSA's unknown order comes from hiding φ(N) (factoring), while class groups aim for unknown order without generating N=p·q.

questions.question: Attack intuition: if an adversary learns the trapdoor (e.g., φ(N) or the factorization of N) for an RSA accumulator, what becomes feasible in many designs?
options: Computing p(x)-th roots mod N, which can enable forging witnesses for elements that were never accumulated
Making membership verification slower than Merkle verification
Converting membership proofs into Schnorr signatures
questions.explanation: Knowing the group order lets you take modular roots by exponentiating with an inverse modulo the order, undermining soundness assumptions that rely on unknown order.

questions.question: In the non-membership proof sketched in this lesson, what condition must hold for x's prime representative relative to s = Π p(y) (product over the set)?
questions.explanation: Bezout coefficients exist for integers s and p(x) only when they are coprime; this is the starting point for the RSA non-membership relation.

questions.question: Which verification check corresponds to the RSA non-membership proof structure shown (with accumulator A = g^s)?
questions.explanation: The proof uses integers a,b such that a·s + b·p(x) = 1. With d = g^b, the verifier checks A^a · d^{p(x)} = g.

questions.question: When should you prefer a Merkle tree over an accumulator for membership proofs?
options: When you want a widely deployed, easy-to-audit construction and can accept logarithmic proof size
When you need constant-size proofs and accept more complex setup/assumptions
When you require an unknown-order group specifically
When you want to avoid hashing entirely
questions.explanation: Merkle trees trade constant-size proofs for simplicity and standardization: proofs scale as O(log n) but updates and audits are straightforward.
